Each February, during National Black History Month, we pause to both celebrate and reflect. It serves as a powerful reminder that black history is American history. It is woven into the foundation of our nation and reflected in its progress.

This year is especially meaningful as we commemorate the 100th anniversary of Black History Month, marking a century since Carter G. Woodson launched Negro History Week in February 1926 to honor the vital role of black history in shaping the American story.

This month and throughout the year, we honor the rich cultural heritage, resilience, achievements, and challenges that continue to shape our communities and our shared future. Here in Henrico County, we remain committed to building onto that legacy through thoughtful investment in our community, our schools, and our students.

We understand that preserving history and advancing opportunities go hand-in-hand, and by strengthening our institutions and expanding access to learning, we work to ensure that every student has the tools, support, and encouragement needed to succeed.

I'm Ryan Young, Vice Chair of the Henrico County School Board, representing the Fairfield District. I want to thank you for the opportunity to speak about Black History Month and about one of Henrico's greatest educational pioneers, Virginia Estelle Randolph.

Black history is not separate from American history. It is woven into the foundation of our schools, our institutions, and the values we teach our children every day. Nowhere is there more visible than on the campus of Virginia Randolph. More than a century ago, Virginia Estelle Randolph stood in a one-room schoolhouse on Mountain Road and imagined something radical for her time.

She believed every child, especially black children, who had been denied opportunity, deserved an education that prepared them to not only survive but to thrive. Randolph began her career as a teacher at the time when opportunity for black educators was scarce. After a short teaching experience in Gooshin County, she taught in Hanover County in 1893 before securing a position with Enrico County the following year.

She opened what became known as the Mountain Road School, a one-room schoolhouse. She personally repaired and restored. She traveled throughout the county, recruiting students, sometimes going door to door, because she believed education was worth it for each and every child. Inside this small schoolhouse, she taught far more than academics.

Randolph introduced woodworking, sewing, gardening, alongside reading and mathematics. She believed manual arts could open employment opportunities for students who might never have access for a secondary education. She involved families and community members directly in the life of the school.

Through school improvement leagues and willing workers clubs, she built pride, responsibility, and ownership in the community. And beyond skills and academics, she believed schools should nurture healthy spirits and strong hearts. She saw education as a pathway to dignity and self-worth. She once described her mission as lifting the children and the community together.

That belief guided everything she did. What she did was not just build a school, it was a model for empowerment. Today, that vision is alive on the campus of Virginia Randolph. The campus is not a monument to the past, it's a living continuation of her work. What makes the campus so powerful is that it reflects the core lesson of black history.

Progress happens when systems adapt to meet the people's needs, not the other way around. On this one campus, Enrico County Public Schools has built a continuum of opportunity intentionally designed to support students and families at every stage of their journey. It begins with the Elementary Intervention Program, ensuring our youngest learners receive early targeted academic support.

The campus also houses the Family and Community Engagement, or the Face Hub, that provides wraparound services and community partnerships. This mirrors Randolph's belief that education is strongest when families are treated as partners, not outsiders. When we strengthen families, we strengthen outcomes. At the secondary level, the Academy of Virginia Randolph offers a high school environment built on restoration, structure, and high expectations.

Students are not defined by a moment, a mistake, or a label by which they were headed. Every student is guided toward being enrolled, employed, or enlisted with dignity and direction. The campus is also home to the Virginia Randolph Education Center, serving students with special needs through individualized instruction grounded in opportunity and respect.

It affirms a simple truth, every learner belongs, every learner deserves access. The Advanced Career Education Center at Virginia Randolph expands opportunities even further. Through ACE programming, students can directly step into high-demand career pathways such as diesel technology, motor sports technology, heavy equipment operation, welding, master barbering, horticulture and plant science, cosmetology and plumbing, and fire sprinkler fitting.

These are real skills, real credentials, and real careers. Students lead with hands-on experience, industry partnerships, and certifications that translate into employment and economic mobility. Together, these programs make the campus something rare. It is a place where intervention, family engagement, specialized education, high school completion, and career readiness exist under one roof.

It's not accidental. It's about intentional design. It's about intentional equity. And that is why the investment in a project like this matters. Henrico County made a nearly $90 million investment in rebuilding and reimagining the campus of Virginia Randolph. That number represents more than construction costs.

It represents a decision to invest in people, in families, and in futures. In this investment and pathways that break cycles and build opportunity, it is a statement that every learner is worth the effort, the resources, and the commitment. More than 100 years ago, Randolph invested her life in children who were told they were not worth it.

Today, we honor her by making the opposite statement. Every child in Henrico County is worth a bold investment. The campus of Virginia Randolph represents a promise, a promise that Henrico County will continue to expand an opportunity, and especially for those historically who had to fight to be seen, heard, and educated.

Our vision empowering every learner is not new. Randolph was living that vision over a century ago. The students we serve today are writing the next chapters of Black History, Henrico History, and American History. Our responsibility is to make sure they have the tools, the support, and the belief in themselves to do it.

That is her legacy, and that is the work that we continue to do each and every day.
